The Named Ice

The same sea ice carries two literatures. One is forty-seven years old, measured in microwave brightness temperature from orbit. The other is older than any instrument, spoken, and precise in ways the satellite is not.
SCROLL
Why this section exists

A satellite sees one thing.

The deck draws sea ice as a number between zero and one: the fraction of a 25-kilometre cell that is frozen. That number is honest, comparable and available every month since November 1978, and it is almost the entire basis on which the world understands what is happening to the poles.

It is also a very thin description. It cannot tell you whether the ice will hold a snowmobile, whether the crack in front of you will close by evening, or whether the edge you are standing on is where the edge was last week. People have needed to know those things for a thousand years, and they built a language that answers them.

What follows is not decoration around the data. It is a second instrument, with a longer record and a finer grain, pointed at the same object. Where it can be quoted from a published source, it is quoted exactly, and the source is named.

Sea-ice terminology · Igloolik, Nunavut

The year in ice

Fifty-nine words for one substance in one place, arranged the way the ice arranges itself: as a year. Not synonyms — states, processes and transitions, each of which changes what a person can safely do.

Made about the ice, and from it

What came back

Almost everything most people know about the poles arrived through a camera, a canvas or a book. It is worth knowing whose — and worth seeing, where the licence allows it to be shown.

Toponymy

Names put back

A map is an argument. In the north, the argument is ongoing, and some of it has recently been won.

The other pole

The continent that nobody is from

The ice was never only a measurement.
It was a road, a boundary, a calendar and an argument about who belongs — long before it was a time series.
